haiku-low.q1: It stores only a SHA-256 hash of the token, in token_hash. The plaintext appears only once, in the create response and the open dialog, never in the database, logs or analytics.
haiku-low.q2: It cannot be recovered. The token is shown once and the server never keeps it, so nobody, including support and engineering, can show it again. The user must create a new token.
haiku-low.q3: The create is refused with a message telling the user to revoke a token first. Nothing is saved and no existing token is replaced.
haiku-low.q4: On the next API call with that token. Every call reads the row, and a revoked token gets 401 at that point.
haiku-low.q5: The same generic 401 body for all three, so the response does not say which one it was. The responses do not differ.
haiku-low.q6: The server SHA-256 hashes the bearer token and finds the row by the unique token_hash index. The row is usable if revoked_at is empty and expires_at is in the future.
haiku-low.q7: Any successful API call with the token triggers it, when last_used_at is empty or over an hour old. The conditional update matches no row if another write already ran, so the database deduplicates.
haiku-low.q8: Nothing happens to the API request. Its response is unaffected, the failure is logged without the token, and last used stays old until a later write succeeds.
haiku-low.q9: Revoking sets revoked_at to now and keeps the row. The list shows active tokens only, so the revoked token disappears from the list.
haiku-low.q10: A token belonging to another user gets 404, the same as a token not found. An already-revoked token: NOT STATED.
haiku-low.q11: A row is left with no one holding the token, and it counts toward the 10-token limit until revoked or expired. The user sees it in the list and can revoke it or create a new token.

sonnet.q1: Only the SHA-256 hash (token_hash column in api_tokens). The plaintext appears only in the create response/open browser dialog, then in the user's own script or CI secret. Never in the database, logs or analytics.
sonnet.q2: They can't. The token is shown once and the server never keeps it; nobody, including support and engineering, can show it again. They must create a new token (and can revoke the old one).
sonnet.q3: The create is refused with a 4xx error telling them to revoke a token first. Nothing is saved or replaced. (Exact status code is an open question.)
sonnet.q4: On the next API call with it: the server reads the row every call (no cache), sees revoked_at set, and returns 401.
sonnet.q5: All get the same 401 with the same generic body. The responses do not differ and don't say which case it was.
sonnet.q6: It SHA-256 hashes the presented token and finds the row by token_hash via the unique index. The row is usable if it exists, has no revoked_at, and expires_at is in the future. The request then runs as the row's user_id.
sonnet.q7: A successful API call where last used is empty or over 1 hour old triggers a background conditional update setting last_used_at to now. The update only applies if the field is still empty or over an hour old, so concurrent duplicates match no row and the database deduplicates.
sonnet.q8: Nothing: the API response is unaffected, never delayed or failed. The failure is logged without the token, and last used stays old until a later write succeeds.
sonnet.q9: It sets revoked_at to now and keeps the row (nothing deleted). The list shows active tokens only, so the revoked token is removed from the list.
sonnet.q10: A token id that is not found or belongs to another user gets 404 (same response for both). NOT STATED for an already revoked token owned by the caller.
sonnet.q11: The row exists (committed), nobody holds the token, and it counts toward the 10-token limit until revoked or expired. The user sees it in the list and can revoke it or create a new token.
